OMISSIONS: Droplets, hands and surfaces as separate routes. They are counted inside non-room-air spread, all of which the model passes face to face.
Infections that spread mainly by hands and surfaces, such as norovirus. Lamps would not be expected to affect them.
Air moving between rooms through corridors and ducts.
New residents arriving, and residents going out.
How ill people become, beyond a fixed share of reported infections ending in a hospital admission. Deaths are not counted, and a resident in hospital stays in the building.
Catching the same infection twice in one season.
Ozone and other by-products that far-UVC lamps add to indoor air.
People behaving differently because lamps are installed.
MISMATCH: Two published numbers are held fixed: how much virus an infected person breathes out (Mikszewski et al. 2022) and the rate of COVID-19 infections reported by US nursing homes in winter 2023-24 (18.7% of residents in 120 days, CDC). With both fixed, how many residents the model infects depends on how much of the spread is non-room-air. At the default, 30%, it infects about 17% of residents, slightly fewer than homes report, and every infection is counted as reported. In the case best for lamps (20%) it infects about 15%. In the cautious case (50%) it infects about 25%, and the gap is closed by assuming that about a quarter of resident infections go unreported. How many infections go unreported has not been measured well.
The virus figure is in quanta, a unit that contains an assumed infectious dose. It is uncertain by a factor of 3 to 10 either way, and the number of infections the model produces moves with it.

Non-room-air spread, the part lamps cannot act on, is set at 30%, with 20% and 50% as the ends of the range. These values come from a calculation and a judgment, not a measurement: no study has measured this split in a nursing home. Published models of a hospital room and a cruise ship put it at 55% and above. Our calculation adjusts them for the lower ventilation of nursing-home bedrooms, which leaves more virus in the room's air. If the true share is above 50%, lamps would do less than any figure shown here. The reasoning and sources are under "How were these numbers chosen?", beside the first slider.

The simulator does not take a separate value of non-room-air spread for each setting, as our calculation does. One strength of face-to-face spread is fitted to the home-wide figure, and the split in each setting follows. At the default it gives 39% for hands-on care in a bedroom, 4% for roommates and 24% for dining and activity rooms, against 40%, 4% and 25% in the calculation.

The model infects about three times as many staff as homes report: 31% to 38% in a season, against about 11%. Either staff infections are heavily under-reported or the model overstates them. Staff counts are shown unadjusted.

One infected staff member arrives every 5 days, on a fixed beat. That rate is our estimate, not a measurement. It was chosen so that the model has a reported resident infection in about as many weeks as US nursing homes did in winter 2023-24: 21% of weeks here, against 15% to 26% of homes in any one week (CDC). Real arrivals are irregular, and visitors and new residents bring infection too. With rarer arrivals the model has fewer, larger outbreaks and lamps prevent more; a slider sets the rate.
An earlier version produced outbreaks that were too short: about three weeks from first to last case, against about eight in published reports. This has not been rechecked.
Rooms are treated as evenly mixed and sealed from one another, which tends to flatter air cleaning in small rooms.

Lamp figures are Illuminate's: how easily far-UVC inactivates the virus, the lamp's output, how far its light travels and how much it must be dimmed. Illuminate works them out for empty rooms of ordinary proportions, here with one to four times one lamp per 250 square feet. Long corridors, odd-shaped rooms and room sizes between those in the table are approximate. On top of that the model counts only three-quarters of the clean air Illuminate computes, which is our judgment.
RSV is not offered: nursing homes have reported it for too short a time, and no one has measured how much of the virus people breathe out.
NOTES: Roommates share their room's air for many hours and spend little of that time face to face. An hour and a half a day makes about 4% of the spread between roommates face to face at the default, which is the figure our calculation gives for roommates.

Spread that reaches a person up close or by hands and surfaces, before far-UVC can act. The rest is room-air spread, which lamps and ventilation remove. The share is counted over infections passed to or from a resident. Our estimate for a nursing home is 30%, with 20% as the case best for lamps and 50% as the cautious one. These come from a calculation and a judgment, not a measurement. In the simulator all of it is passed face to face, and moving this slider re-fits the strength of that. It also changes how many residents the model infects: about 15% at 0.20, 17% at 0.30 and 25% at 0.50, against the 18.7% that homes report to CDC. Above about 0.36 the model infects more than homes report and the extra is taken to go unreported; below it the model infects slightly fewer. Lamps help less when this share is higher.

From the estimate for SARS-CoV-2 at rest by Mikszewski et al. 2022, whose final paper gives 0.55; the model uses 0.52, from an earlier version. A dose here infects about 63% of people who take it in. Uncertain by a factor of 3 to 10 either way. The strength of face-to-face spread and the share of infections reported were worked out at 0.52 and are not re-fitted when you move this.

Speaking releases about five times as much virus as quiet breathing (Mikszewski et al. 2022). Set to 2 because residents in shared rooms speak only part of the time, and so that the published virus output and the CDC infection rate can both hold. Applies to residents outside their room, visitors and staff on break.
Set to 5, the same as continuous talking: care work is light activity with intermittent talking.

Set to 0.5, the top of our range, so that the published virus output and the CDC infection rate can both hold. Past infection protected about 36-45% against reinfection, waning over months (COVID-19 Forecasting Team 2023); fewer than a third of residents had the latest vaccine.

US nursing homes reported 5.8 COVID-19 hospital admissions for every 109.3 reported infections in winter 2023-24: 5.3% (Franklin et al. 2024). Other estimates run from about 4% (English care homes, early 2022) to about 6.5% (US, October 2024). Applied to reported infections only, however the resident was infected.

Illuminate, the lamp-planning tool from OSLUV, gives the average distance a wall-mounted lamp's light travels through a room's air. Angled down, that is about 3.6 metres in a single bedroom and 6.2 in a dining room; pointed straight across, about 2.4 and 5.3. This slider scales the figure, since furniture and people may shorten or lengthen it.

Illuminate's exposure check (ANSI/IES RP-27.1-22, with the ACGIH limits) finds how far each room's lamps must be dimmed so that no point at head height gets more than the limit in 8 hours. It allows a lamp angled down full output under ceilings of 2.7 m or more, about 90% at 2.6 m, about half at 2.4 m and about 30% at 2.3 m. That agrees with the maker's mounting rule once the lamp is taken to hang 10 cm below the ceiling. Pointed straight across the room, a lamp may run at about 90% at 2.4 m and about 60% at 2.3 m. More lamps in a room mean a little more dimming for each. Turning this off overstates what a compliant installation delivers.

Outdoor air plus filtered air supplied to a room, counted in room-volumes an hour. This slider moves every room together. At the default, bedrooms get 1.5, corridors and nurses' stations 2, dining rooms and lounges 3, the therapy room 4 and the staff break room 1. Those defaults are our judgment. They sit below the design minimums (2 for bedrooms, 4 for most shared rooms; ASHRAE 170) because older buildings often fall short. Each kind of room has its own slider under Building.

Staff wear no masks day to day. All working staff wear surgical masks while outbreak measures are in force, except in the break room: from the day after the first person with symptoms on any wing until 14 days after the latest. In a default COVID-19 winter that is about three days in four. This slider scales the mask's effect during those periods. 0.7 is within the 50-90% range used in transmission studies; masks slip down to talk, eat or drink.

NOTES_FLU: transmission.closeShare

Influenza has no figure of its own. Each case uses the same strength of face-to-face spread as COVID-19, and the split is what the model then gives: 25% at the default, 16% in the case best for lamps and 46% in the cautious one. Moving this re-fits both that strength and the virus breathed out, so the model still infects about 6.9% of residents a season. Hands, surfaces and large droplets are thought to matter more for influenza than for COVID-19, and one risk model of the routes leaves little of influenza's spread to room air (Nicas & Jones 2009). If that is right, the share is well above this range and lamps would do much less than shown. A hospital study of ultraviolet air disinfection in the 1957-58 pandemic points the other way (McLean, in Tellier 2006), and a household study put about half of spread in aerosols (Cowling et al. 2013).
emission.activity.social

Speaking releases about five times as much virus as quiet breathing (Mikszewski et al. 2022). Set to 2, as for COVID-19, because residents in shared rooms speak only part of the time. Applies to residents outside their room, visitors and staff on break.
emission.activity.work
Set to 5, the same as continuous talking: care work is light activity with intermittent talking.
immune.protection
About 58% of residents were vaccinated in 2025-26, and the vaccine was about 30% effective in people over 65 that season (CDC). A little is added for past infection.
immune.protectionStaff
About 40% of nursing home staff were vaccinated in 2025-26, and the vaccine was about 35% effective in working-age adults (CDC). Some is added for past infection.
severity.pHospital

US nursing homes reported about one hospital admission for every five reported influenza infections in both 2024-25 and 2025-26 (CDC NHSN). That is about four times the COVID-19 figure; part of the gap is that milder influenza is tested for less often. Applied to reported infections only, however the resident was infected.
disease.latent.mean
0.9 days in US households (Chan et al. 2025).
disease.presymptomatic.mean
0.7 days in US households. About 16% of influenza spread happens before symptoms, against about half for COVID-19 (Chan et al. 2025).
disease.infectious.mean

Infectiousness falls from the first day of symptoms, so 3 days here is worth about 2 days at full strength, the figure fitted to US household data (Chan et al. 2025). Virus can be detected for nearly 5 days (Carrat et al. 2008), but the tail spreads little. No one has measured this in frail older people.
disease.asymRelInf

In 727 Hong Kong households during the 2009 pandemic, infected people without symptoms were 0.57 times as infectious as those with symptoms. The 95% interval runs from 0.11 to 1.54, so the study cannot rule out that they are equally infectious (Tsang et al. 2023).
disease.pSymptomatic.resident
No study of influenza without symptoms in older adults was found. Set as for COVID-19.
disease.pSymptomatic.staff

Among healthcare workers, about 40% of influenza infections in the unvaccinated and 75% in the vaccinated had symptoms (Kuster et al. 2011). One hospital study found far fewer with clear symptoms (Bénet et al. 2021). In Hong Kong households in 2009, 60% of infected adults had at least one symptom (Tsang et al. 2023).
control.staffExclusion.exclusionDays
CDC advises that staff with influenza stay off work until at least a day after their fever ends. Five days is our allowance for that.
control.outbreakMode.outbreakDays
CDC advises keeping outbreak measures for at least 7 days after the latest confirmed case.
emission.gsd

In the published estimate, influenza varies less between people than SARS-CoV-2 (Mikszewski et al. 2022). The heaviest shedder measured (Bueno de Mesquita et al. 2020) is far beyond what this spread allows, so it may be too narrow.
control.maskCompliance

Staff wear no masks day to day. All working staff wear surgical masks while outbreak measures are in force, except in the break room: from the day after the second case within three days on a wing until 7 days after the latest. In a default influenza winter that is under a tenth of days. This slider scales the mask's effect during those periods. 0.7 is within the 50-90% range used in transmission studies; masks slip down to talk, eat or drink.
INTRO: Where studies support a range, the slider spans it. Otherwise the value and its range are our judgment, and the source line says so. The first six matter most. Three settings were moved to make the model fit. With the published figure for the virus a person breathes out and the values studies suggest for these three, the model would infect more residents than nursing homes report to CDC. To close that gap, residents are taken to talk less than studies suggest (2 times their resting output, not 5), staff at work to breathe out less (5 times, the bottom of our range) and existing immunity to protect more (0.5, the top of our range). With these settings the model infects about as many residents as homes report at the default, or slightly fewer.
INTRO_FLU: Where studies support a range, the slider spans it. Otherwise the value and its range are our judgment, and the source line says so. The first six matter most. Influenza rests on weaker ground than COVID-19. Nursing homes have reported it to CDC only since 2025, and the published figure for the virus a person breathes out is too low to produce the influenza they report, so the model fits that figure.
MISMATCH_FLU: Two things are held fixed: the rate of influenza infections reported by US nursing homes in winter 2025-26 (2.3% of residents in 120 days; our calculation from CDC's NHSN data, the first complete season of reporting) and one infected staff member arriving every 8 days. The winter before was worse, at about 4%.

The published estimate of the virus a person with influenza breathes out (0.035 quanta an hour at rest, Mikszewski et al. 2022) gives the model less than a third of the infections homes report. So the model fits that number: 0.69 at the default, about 20 times the published figure. Published estimates run from 0.035 to 0.17 for a typical person and into the hundreds for the heaviest shedders. The published figure fits the reported infections only if more than nine-tenths of spread is non-room-air, in which case lamps would do little.
The model assumes one influenza infection in three is reported. No study has measured this in nursing homes; 3 is our choice from a range of 2 to 5.

Influenza has no separate figure for non-room-air spread. It uses the same strength of face-to-face spread as COVID-19, which gives 25% at the default and 16% to 46% across the range. That rests on weaker ground than the COVID-19 figure. Hands, surfaces and large droplets are thought to matter more for influenza, and a risk model of the routes puts most of its spread there (Nicas & Jones 2009); if so, lamps would do much less than shown. A hospital study of ultraviolet air disinfection in the 1957-58 pandemic points the other way.

How easily far-UVC inactivates airborne influenza has been measured twice, and the results differ eleven-fold (1.8 and 19 in Illuminate's table). The default, 10.4, is their midpoint, following Illuminate's rule of taking the median. No measurement sits near it.

Antiviral prophylaxis is not modelled. CDC advises oseltamivir for the residents of a unit once two cases are confirmed there. Where that is done promptly it prevents some of the same infections lamps would, so the lamp effect is overstated for those homes. In usual practice it is given in a minority of seasons.
In the model about a quarter of seasons see a tenth or more of residents infected, and a typical one of those reaches 16%. Published outbreak reports give 33%, but they favour large outbreaks.
With about 2.6 reported infections a season among 112 residents, 200 simulated seasons leave the percentages uncertain by a few points.
Rooms are treated as evenly mixed and sealed from one another, which tends to flatter air cleaning in small rooms.

Lamp figures are Illuminate's: how easily far-UVC inactivates the virus, the lamp's output, how far its light travels and how much it must be dimmed. Illuminate works them out for empty rooms of ordinary proportions, here with one to four times one lamp per 250 square feet. Long corridors, odd-shaped rooms and room sizes between those in the table are approximate. On top of that the model counts only three-quarters of the clean air Illuminate computes, which is our judgment.
BRIEF: transmission.closeShare
Spread that reaches a person up close or by hands and surfaces, before far-UVC can act. The rest is room-air spread, which lamps and ventilation remove.
emission.median
Counted in infectious doses an hour, for a typical infected person breathing quietly. One dose infects about 63% of the people who take it in.
emission.gsd
A few people breathe out most of the virus. A larger number here means a wider gap between a typical person and the heaviest emitters.
emission.activity.social
How many times more virus a person breathes out while talking than at rest. It applies to residents outside their room, visitors and staff on break.
transmission.beta.care
How fast the pocket of air between a carer and a resident is flushed. Lower values mean riskier close contact.
transmission.roommateHours
Time each day that roommates are close enough to count as face to face, on top of sharing their room's air.
air.decay
The rate at which airborne virus loses its ability to infect by itself, before lamps or ventilation are counted.
importation.arrivalEveryDays
One staff member, infected outside work, arrives on a fixed beat. This is how infection enters the home in the model.
lamp.susceptibility
How much of the airborne virus a given amount of far-UVC light inactivates. A higher value means lamps clean the air faster.
lamp.aimAcross
Lamps are mounted high on the walls. They can be angled down into the room or pointed straight across it.
lamp.pathFactor
Scales the average distance a lamp's light travels through a room's air. A longer path means more air is cleaned.
lamp.followMountingRule
Whether each room's lamps are dimmed so that no point at head height gets more than the exposure limit in 8 hours.
lamp.bedroomShare
How far bedroom lamps are turned down because residents spend much longer than 8 hours a day there. At 1 they run as in any other room.
lamp.realWorldFactor
The lamp calculation assumes an empty, evenly mixed room. This is the share of that clean air counted in a real one.
transmission.nearFieldUV
How much lamps reduce the dose passed directly between two people who are face to face. Zero means not at all.
ventilation.scale
Outdoor air plus filtered air supplied to a room, counted in room-volumes an hour. This slider moves every room together.
facility.ach.bedroom
Outdoor air plus filtered air supplied to each bedroom, counted in room-volumes an hour.
people.mobility.communal
Residents who leave their rooms for meals and activities. The three resident shares are scaled to add up to one.
staff.careMinutes
How long a carer stays with a resident on each visit for washing, dressing and similar help.
disease.presymptomatic.mean
The average time an infected person can pass the virus on before they feel ill.
disease.infectious.mean
The average time a person stays infectious once their symptoms have started.
disease.pSymptomatic.resident
Of the residents who are infected, the share who feel ill. The rest are infected without symptoms.
disease.pSymptomatic.staff
Of the staff who are infected, the share who feel ill. The rest are infected without symptoms.
disease.asymRelInf
An infected person who never has symptoms breathes out this fraction of the virus that a person with symptoms does.
severity.pHospital
The share of reported resident infections that end in a hospital admission. It is the same however the resident was infected.
immune.protection
How much protection from past infection and vaccines lowers the dose that counts for a resident. At 0.5 the dose is halved.
control.maskCompliance
Staff wear surgical masks only while outbreak measures are in force. This slider scales the mask's effect during those periods.
